How to use the Salary Calculator

  1. Enter your pay and choose the period it covers.
  2. Adjust hours per day, days per week and paid weeks per year to match your contract.
  3. Press Convert to see the equivalent in every other period.

Why "paid weeks per year" changes everything

A salaried employee is normally paid for all 52 weeks, including holidays. A contractor who takes four weeks off unpaid is paid for 48. Comparing their rates without adjusting for this overstates the contractor's income by about 8%.

The standard full-time year is 2,080 hours — 40 hours × 52 weeks. This is the figure behind most quick conversions, including the familiar shortcut of halving an hourly rate and reading it as thousands per year: $30/hour ≈ $60,000/year.

Comparing an offer honestly

Two roles with identical salaries can differ substantially in what they actually pay per hour. Before comparing, normalise for:

  • Contracted hours. A 37.5-hour week is 6% more per hour than a 40-hour week at the same salary.
  • Unpaid overtime. Salaried roles that routinely run to 50 hours cut the effective rate by a fifth.
  • Paid leave and public holidays. Six weeks off is worth roughly 12% of salary against a role with two.
  • Employer pension contributions, bonuses and benefits, none of which appear in the headline figure.

Frequently asked questions

Why is monthly pay not four times weekly?

A month averages 4.33 weeks. Multiplying weekly pay by four understates annual income by about 8%. This tool divides annual pay by 12 instead, which is exact.

Does it calculate take-home pay?

No. Net pay depends on your tax jurisdiction, allowances, pension contributions and personal circumstances. Use your national tax authority's calculator for an accurate net figure.

How do I work out an overtime rate?

Take the hourly figure and multiply by your overtime multiplier — typically 1.5 for time-and-a-half or 2 for double time.

What if my hours vary week to week?

Use your average over a representative few months. For irregular work, enter a realistic annual total in the hours fields rather than a typical good week.
